selection.method: next 10 verified actor-primary profiles after Batch 16

profiles.name: Rube Weiss
profiles.excerpt: Rube Weiss was a Detroit radio actor whose villain roles on The Lone Ranger grew into a long voiceover career heard in major national advertising and narration.
profiles.bio_html:
Rube Weiss belonged to the professional Detroit acting community that supplied WXYZ adventure programs with much of their supporting cast. He and his wife, Liz Weiss, both worked in local radio and television, and Rube was especially useful on The Lone Ranger as a rotating gallery of villains and other character roles.

Weiss's voice later became a profession in its own right beyond dramatic radio. He recorded national and regional commercial work, including advertising and promotional narration, and remained a recognizable Detroit voice for decades. That sustained work supports a second GRH category for commercial and sponsor performance.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 23 The Lone Ranger performances credited to Weiss and one Challenge of the Yukon appearance. Those broadcasts preserve the WXYZ dramatic foundation of the voice career that followed.

profiles.name: Sid Raymond
profiles.excerpt: Sid Raymond turned a gift for comic voices into a career that stretched from Duffy's Tavern to animation and nationally seen commercial characters.
profiles.bio_html:
Sid Raymond was born Raymond Silverstein in Manhattan in 1909 and entered entertainment through resort and touring work before becoming a durable radio, television and voice actor. His comic delivery made him especially effective as characters who sounded instantly recognizable even without a visual introduction.

Raymond took over the role of Finnegan on Duffy's Tavern during the program's final seasons and later became widely heard as the voice of Baby Huey and other animated characters. Commercial performance became another major branch of his career, including a long run as a comic bartender in Schlitz advertising, so sponsor work is retained as a genuine second category.

Golden Radio Hour's detailed relationship data currently preserves 44 Duffy's Tavern performances credited to Raymond and one X Minus One appearance. The corrected total of 45 replaces an older 24-episode summary in the routing data.

profiles.name: Bill Lipton
profiles.excerpt: Bill Lipton was a New York radio repertory actor whose surviving work is strongest in Johnny Dollar and X Minus One.
profiles.bio_html:
Bill Lipton belongs to the New York radio repertory whose professional record is preserved more fully in cast lists and recordings than in later biographical accounts. He worked in dramatic broadcasting across crime, anthology and science-fiction programs during the 1950s and 1960s.

Lipton appeared repeatedly on Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar and X Minus One, with additional work on The Chase, Columbia Workshop and Gang Busters. Those credits place him in the flexible supporting company network radio depended on as regular dramatic series became less common.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 14 Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances credited to Lipton, five X Minus One appearances, two The Chase episodes and additional work on Columbia Workshop and Gang Busters.

profiles.name: Len Doyle
profiles.excerpt: Len Doyle made investigator Harrington on Mr. District Attorney a thirteen-year radio role, choosing the microphone even when stage opportunities competed for his time.
profiles.bio_html:
Len Doyle was born in Toledo in 1893, trained at the American Academy of Dramatic Arts and worked in stock and Broadway theatre before radio gave him the role that defined his career. He also spent time as a professional boxer, part of a varied path to broadcasting.

Doyle joined Mr. District Attorney as investigator Harrington and remained with the part for roughly thirteen years, eventually carrying it into television. Contemporary accounts noted that stage productions sometimes arranged schedules around his radio commitment because Doyle preferred continuing the broadcast role.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 22 Mr. District Attorney performances credited to Doyle and one Columbia Workshop appearance. Harrington is therefore the clear center of his surviving GRH radio profile.

profiles.name: Monty Margetts
profiles.excerpt: Monty Margetts moved from radio acting into pioneering live television hosting, turning an improvised cooking program into one of early Los Angeles television's personality-driven hits.
profiles.bio_html:
Monty Margetts was born in Vancouver in 1912 and began working as an actress in radio before moving into film and television. Her radio credits show the broad repertory training that preceded the part of her career for which Los Angeles viewers later remembered her best.

In the early television era, Margetts became the host of a live cooking program built around her own comic lack of culinary expertise. She later recalled that mistakes, improvisation and audience curiosity became the show's appeal. Because hosting became a substantial profession rather than an occasional appearance, it is retained as a second category in her GRH profile.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 11 NBC University Theater performances credited to Margetts, five each on The Whistler and Wild Bill Hickok, and additional appearances on Screen Directors Playhouse and The Adventures of Frank Race.

profiles.name: Olan Soule
profiles.excerpt: Olan Soule was one of radio's great utility actors, accumulating thousands of broadcasts and commercials before becoming a familiar television face and the animated voice of Batman.
profiles.bio_html:
Olan Soule was born in Illinois in 1909 and entered professional theatre with a touring tent company before moving into Chicago radio in the early 1930s. He became a regular on Bachelor's Children and later spent years as the male lead on First Nighter, developing a reputation for a voice that could sound far larger and more imposing than his slight physical build.

Soule eventually accumulated thousands of radio performances and commercials, then carried that versatility into television, film and animation. Later audiences knew him from Dragnet and as the voice of Batman in Super Friends. His extensive commercial work is substantial enough to remain a second professional category.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves five Sears Radio Theater performances credited to Soule, three each on Lux Radio Theatre and The Great Gildersleeve, two each on Have Gun, Will Travel, The Adventures of Philip Marlowe, The Whistler and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, plus additional dramatic work.

profiles.name: Paul McVey
profiles.excerpt: Paul McVey was a veteran character actor whose radio work crossed westerns, literary anthology and crime drama alongside a long screen career.
profiles.bio_html:
Paul McVey was born in Boston in 1898 and built a long career as a supporting actor in film, television and radio. Screen audiences saw him in pictures ranging from Force of Evil to Shane, while radio used the same steady character presence across several dramatic genres.

McVey appeared in westerns, literary adaptations and crime programs, moving among productions such as Tales of the Texas Rangers, NBC University Theater, Wild Bill Hickok and Escape. His radio work fits the pattern of a professional character actor valued for reliability rather than a single continuing part.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves four performances each on Screen Directors Playhouse and Tales of the Texas Rangers credited to McVey, three each on NBC University Theater and Wild Bill Hickok, two each on Escape, Lux Radio Theatre and This Is Your FBI, plus additional work on Broadway Is My Beat.

profiles.name: Walter Catlett
profiles.excerpt: Walter Catlett carried decades of vaudeville, Broadway and film comedy into radio, where his excitable character style remained instantly recognizable.
profiles.bio_html:
Walter Catlett was born in San Francisco in 1889 and began his professional career in vaudeville before moving into Broadway and film. He became one of Hollywood's great comic character actors, specializing in pompous, excitable and officious men whose confidence usually exceeded their judgment.

Radio made use of the same rapid delivery and comic agitation that defined Catlett's screen work. His career reached across stage, film and broadcasting, and his best-known later voice performance was J. Worthington Foulfellow in Disney's Pinocchio.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 21 This Is Your FBI performances credited to Catlett, along with appearances on Escape and The Line Up. Those broadcasts preserve a substantial radio chapter within a career that began onstage before World War I.

profiles.name: Ed Emerson
profiles.excerpt: Ed Emerson was a regular Lux Radio Theatre stock actor whose supporting work helped weekly Hollywood adaptations sound fully populated around their guest stars.
profiles.bio_html:
Ed Emerson belonged to the professional supporting company surrounding Lux Radio Theatre during the 1940s. Personal biography is sparsely documented, but contemporary production coverage identifies him among the program's working actors and shows him participating in the demanding weekly routine behind one of network radio's largest dramatic productions.

Lux adaptations regularly centered major film stars, but the broadcasts depended on stock actors such as Emerson to handle smaller roles, doubles and scene-setting characters around them. Surviving cast records place him in productions including Mister Lucky, Casablanca, Made for Each Other and other feature-film adaptations.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 22 Lux Radio Theatre performances credited to Emerson. That concentrated holding documents the supporting-company work that formed the clearest surviving part of his radio career.

profiles.name: Gloria Holiday
profiles.excerpt: Gloria Holiday was a radio comedy actress whose Bessie on The Great Gildersleeve and later work with Harold Peary placed her inside two closely related network ensembles.
profiles.bio_html:
Gloria Holiday became a familiar radio comedy performer during the later years of The Great Gildersleeve. She played Bessie, Gildersleeve's well-meaning but inept secretary, a recurring part that placed her inside the everyday comic life of Summerfield.

Holiday married original Gildersleeve star Harold Peary and later worked in the ensemble of The Harold Peary Show, where she played Gloria, part of the new small-town world built around Peary after his move to CBS. Her radio career therefore extended beyond one supporting role into a second continuing comedy company.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 20 The Great Gildersleeve performances credited to Holiday, along with appearances on Lux Radio Theatre and Sealtest Variety Theater. Those holdings document the Bessie role at the center of her GRH profile.
